implementation_notes: System.Lazy<T> is the BCL's realization of both the guard and the cache: construct it with the acquisition delegate and the delegate runs on the first Value access. The default mode for the delegate constructor is LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication, which makes the first reader acquire under a lock and publishes the value to everyone else; PublicationOnly lets racing callers run the factory and keeps whichever finishes first, which is only safe for idempotent acquisitions; None is for holders that never leave one thread. The classic structure is still what you write when the resource must be released or re-done, because Lazy<T> is one-shot: a holder with Reset/Dispose (or a Lazy<IDisposable> plus an owner) replaces it. For asynchronous acquisition, wrap a Task - Lazy<Task<T>> triggers one acquisition and the task is the shared result.
pitfalls: With ExecutionAndPublication a failed acquisition is cached: every later access rethrows the original exception, so a transient outage poisons the Lazy for the life of the process; re-create the Lazy (or use a retrying factory with PublicationOnly) when retry matters.
Accessing Value from inside its own valueFactory throws InvalidOperationException - the acquisition path must never touch the Lazy field it is initializing.
PublicationOnly can run the factory several times on first use; if acquisition has side effects (sockets, licenses, file locks) use ExecutionAndPublication and pay the lock.
In a DI container, injecting Lazy<T> into a singleton captures the singleton's scope: if T is scoped, the Lazy becomes a captive dependency with the lifetime mismatch that implies.

variants.name: Asynchronous Lazy<Task<T>>
variants.implementation_notes: There is no asynchronous Lazy<T>: the idiom is to make the lazily acquired value a Task - Lazy<Task<T>> whose factory starts the asynchronous acquisition on first Value access, or a lazily created Task field guarded by a lock (the AsyncLazy pattern). The task memoizes both success and failure, and because the factory only *creates* the task, the mode's lock is held for a moment rather than for the whole I/O.
pitfalls: A faulted Lazy<Task<T>> is as sticky as its synchronous sibling: awaiting it again rethrows the same exception unless the field is replaced with a new task.
Do not await inside the factory: with ExecutionAndPublication that serializes unrelated work behind the lock and can deadlock in contexts with a synchronization context.
A cached task created in one DI scope and consumed from another captures the creating scope's services - resolve per scope or pass dependencies as arguments.
